books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Challenging Child Labor
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Lewis Hine, photographs of child workers, c. 1908-1911

stimulus.source_note: Photograph by Lewis Hine, c. 1911, public domain (pre-1930). Caption per the source record.
stimulus.text: Photograph by Lewis Hine, 1911. A young girl in a plain dress stands outdoors and looks directly at the camera. Hine's caption records her as a girl working in a cannery.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: The photograph best supports which conclusion about Progressive reform?

options.text: Reformers used vivid evidence to make distant problems feel personal to readers
Child labor ended everywhere as soon as the photograph was published
options.misconception: Child labor continued for decades; the Keating-Owen Act of 1916 was struck down, and federal standards came only in the 1930s.

options.text: Photographers replaced lawmakers as the leaders of reform
options.misconception: Photographs built pressure, but laws still had to pass Congress and survive the courts.

options.text: Most Americans already knew exactly how bad child labor was
options.misconception: If most Americans had known, Hine's photographs would not have shocked them; his work was news to middle-class readers.

rationales.A: Hine's portrait puts one young face in front of the reader instead of a statistic. Progressives used photographs exactly this way: to make a distant problem personal enough that middle-class readers demanded action.
rationales.B: One photograph did not end child labor. The Keating-Owen Act came five years later and was struck down in 1918.
rationales.C: Photographers supplied evidence, not laws. Congress and the courts still decided what became law.
rationales.D: Hine's photographs were news precisely because most middle-class Americans had never seen a cannery floor or a mill.
rationales.general:
1. Look at what the photograph does. One young girl, facing the camera, becomes a person instead of a number.
2. Ask why reformers published such pictures. Vivid evidence moved middle-class readers who had never seen a cannery floor.
3. Check the overclaims. One photograph did not end child labor or replace lawmakers.
Remember: evidence persuades by making the abstract concrete, so ask what a picture lets a reader feel that a statistic cannot.

figures.caption: Lewis Hine, girl working in a cannery, 1911. A young girl in a plain dress stands outdoors and faces the camera.
figures.alt: A sepia portrait of a young girl in a plain dress with an embroidered collar, standing outdoors and looking at the camera.
